newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - Palladium supply seen down, demand up in 97.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Palladium supply seen down, demand up in 97.

text.p: Russian palladium stockpiles were run down further by a surge in Russian exports in 1996, but rising demand for the white metal from the automotive industry will keep the market tight in 1997, analysts said.

"Based on a ten year model of Russian mine output, domestic demand and exports, we estimate Russian palladium inventories could be down to obout two million ounces, or less than one year's worth of exports," said Jeffrey Christian, managing director of New York based consultants, CPM Group.

Other analysts think Russia could still have several years worth of palladium exports in inventories, but agree the surplus of supply over demand is seen contracting for the first time in seven years.
Russia supplies about 60 percent of the world's palladium, but the size of its palladium stockpile is a closely-guarded state secret.
Spot palladium prices rose about 35 percent in the first two months of the year to around $160 an ounce, the highest level since June 1995, before falling back to $145 this week.
RUSSIAN SUPPLIES SEEN FALLING IN 1997:

CPM Group estimated Russian palladium mine output in 1996 at 2.52 million ounces, while exports were estimated at 3.95 million ounces, or over 150 percent of mine output, leading to a further draw-down of Russian stockpiles.
Refiner Johnson Matthey estimated exports at 3.8 million ounces last year, while industry analysts CRU International estimated 1996 exports rose to 4.2 million ounces.

"The Russians have been shipping maybe twice their annual mine production for several years now, so the question of how much they will export in 1997 is the key issue," said John Brimelow, New York based director of international equities for German bank, BV Capital.
Earlier this month an official with Russia's metal export agency, Almaz, said there would be no shipments of palladium to Japan in March, and indicated Russian exports to Japan would fall this year.
Japan accounts for about 40 percent of palladium demand.

Shipments of Russian palladium to Japan were suspended after talks on an annual supply contract broke down in December 1996, though some imports of Russian origin were reported in Japan's January import data.
"Japanese imports in January were only hallmarked of Russian origin but were exported earlier," Johnson Matthey's manager of precious metals marketing, Jeremy Coombs, said.
But last week the deputy chief executive of Almaz, Alexander Kulichkov, said shipments may resume soon.
"Russia could start making spot sales of palladium to Japan again soon, but most sales occur under contract and will probably not begin until at least May," Coombs said.

"Contract shipments are based on the monthly average price, and notice provisions mean the next shipment would be based on April's average price, so it could be May before palladium would ship to Japan," he said.
AUTO DEMAND SEEN UP:
Meanwhile, demand for palladium for use in automotive emissions catalysts is seen rising, helped by a switch from platinum to palladium catalysts, led by Ford Motor Co.
The auto industry accounts for about 25 percent of palladium demand, while semi-conductors and electronics applications account for about 50 percent.
Last week General Motors Corp and Chrysler Corp both denied making any changes to their palladium purchasing program after the recent rise in palladium prices.

"Despite the recent price rise, palladium is probably still good value, as we expect Russian palladium exports this year to be down 10-15 percent on last year, while we are revising up our estimates of auto sector demand," CPM Group analyst Ted Kempf said.
Russian palladium exports to the U.S. jumped 77 percent to 1.88 million ounces in the January-November 1996 period, according to CRU Internatioanl.
"Deliveries of palladium into US were high last year, especially in the last quarter," CRU International analyst Tony Warwick-Ching said.
"But we believe you should look at the 1996-97 period as a whole and think last year's exports were pre-shipments of some kind, so Russian supplies could be lower in 1997," he said.
"But its true automotive demand has risen about threefold in two years, and electronics demand is also buoyant, while there is talk of hedge funds accumulating positions," he said.
HEDGE FUND INVOLVEMENT:
New York based hedge fund, Tiger Management, run by Julian Robertson, with $8.5 billion under management, has confirmed it is a player in the palladium market.
"We stand by Mr Robertson's recent comments to Institutional Investor magazine and Barron's," a spokesman for Tiger Management told Reuters.
"We started buying palladium last year and our basic view is bullish for the next two or three years."

Earlier Robertson told Institutional Investor magazine and the weekly Barrons he thought palladium prices could go up 80 percent to $200-300 an ounce before substitution for platinum would occur as the palladium supply/demand balance was heading into a shortfall.
